terms.grammar: conjunction, after a comparative: what is compared stands in the same case on both sides
evidence: Sen. Ep. 47.2: ēst ille plūs quam capit
Publ. R 24: Rogantī melius quam imperantī pāreās.
terms.comment: With magis … quam and potius … quam, “rather than”. With numbers, plūs, amplius, minus often stand without quam (Lewis & Short s.v. plus).

terms.grammar: the second term in the ablative, without quam
evidence: Varr. RR 3.7.4: nihil enim timidius columbā
Mart. 13.81.1–2: rhombus lātior est tamen patellā
terms.comment: Where the first term is in the nominative or accusative, the second may go into the ablative instead: lātior patellā, wider than the dish. Commonest in short, fixed comparisons and after a negative (nihil … columbā).

phrases.english: he eats more than he can hold
One obeys a person who asks better than one who orders.

phrases.latin: nē plūs cēnseat sapere sē quam dominum
phrases.english: let him not think he knows more than his master
for nothing is more timid than a dove

phrases.latin: quamvīs lāta gerat patella rhombum, rhombus lātior est tamen patellā
phrases.english: however wide the dish that holds the turbot, the turbot is wider than the dish
